cues.text: Two Christian Traditions, One Kingdom
By the mid-seventh century, the kingdom of Northumbria in northern England found itself home to two distinct Christian traditions living uneasily side by side.
A native Celtic Christianity was carried to Northumbria by Irish missionaries from Iona, observing its own customs for calculating Easter and the tonsure of monks.
The Roman tradition, introduced more recently by missionaries sent from Rome, followed a different Easter calculation entirely.
The disagreement produced the awkward practical spectacle of the Northumbrian royal court itself sometimes celebrating Easter on two different dates within the same household.
A King Calls a Council
King Oswiu of Northumbria summoned representatives of both parties to a synod at the double monastery of Whitby in 664.
His wife followed the Roman observance, while he himself had been raised in the Celtic tradition.
The synod, presided over by the abbess St. Hilda , was convened to settle the dispute once and for all rather than allow the kingdom's religious practice to remain permanently divided.
Peter's Keys
The Celtic party, represented chiefly by Bishop Colman , defended their Easter calculation as tradition handed down from St. John the Evangelist himself through St. Columba.
The Roman party, represented by Wilfrid , argued for the calculation used by the wider universal Church, tracing it ultimately to St. Peter’s authority.
When Oswiu asked directly whether Christ had truly given Peter the keys of heaven, both sides answered affirmatively.
The king declared he would not risk offending the doorkeeper who held the keys to the kingdom he himself hoped to enter.
A Kingdom Aligns with Rome
Oswiu's ruling settled the matter decisively in favor of the Roman observance, and Northumbria adopted the Roman Easter calculation and tonsure from that point forward.
Bishop Colman, unwilling to abandon the tradition of his own teachers, withdrew from Northumbria with a number of Celtic monks who shared his conviction.
They retreated first to Iona and eventually to Ireland rather than conform to the new practice—a quiet, voluntary exile rather than any formal condemnation or schism.
Legacy
Whitby's decision aligned the whole of the English Church with continental and Roman practice at a formative moment in its development.
It smoothed the way for the closer administrative unity St. Theodore of Tarsus would bring to the English dioceses as Archbishop of Canterbury only a few years later.

The synod remains, in the memory of English Christianity, the decisive moment when the youthful Church of England chose deliberately, after frank debate rather than simple drift, to root its future life firmly within the wider communion of Rome.
